q: Krystyna learned how to make szarlotka (pronounced “shar-LOT-ka”) from her grandmother decades ago and has been making it ever since. […] Make the szarlotka a day before you want to serve it. It’s far better after an overnight rest at room temperature, because then the pastry and apples meld together into a unified whole.
2007 November 30, Greg Patent, “Szarlotka”, in A Baker’s Odyssey: Celebrating Time-Honored Recipes from America’s Rich Immigrant Heritage, Hoboken, N.J.: John Wiley & Sons, →ISBN, page 138:

The enticing, homey scent of apple pie wafted into the hallway as she beckoned them into her lair. […] “Something smells delicious,” Cam said. He sniffed the air, practically drooling. / “I just took a szarlotka out of the oven.”
2011 April 12, Beth Kendrick, chapter 29, in The Bake-Off, New York, N.Y.: New American Library, →ISBN:

There’s almost no Polish family without a szarlotka recipe—a short-crust apple pie with either a crumble or a second layer of pastry and occasionally a meringue topping. […] To prepare the base of the szarlotka, roll out your dough on a lightly floured work surface into a rectangle about the size of the pan.
2025 October 14, Laurel Kratochvila, “Szarlotka: Shortcrust Apple Cake”, in Dobre Dobre: Baking from Poland and Beyond, San Francisco, Calif.: Chronicle Books, →ISBN:

e:
Named in 1861 by Karl Ferdinand Peters in honour of Stephen Szaibely (1777-1855), mine surveyor of Rézbánya, Hungary, now Romania.
Szaibely + -ite
